#2177. Como vs Man Utd Preview: Team news, injuries, form and where to watch

Shumail Sajid writes about Manchester United for Read Man Utd and Crystal Palace for Read Crystal Palace, with occasional pieces on other Premier League clubs. He has also written for FanSided's Red Devils Dispatch, Yardbarker, Anfield Central and The Sports Side.

Manchester United travel to Italy on Wednesday, looking for their first win since September 10, when they face Como in the Champions League.

Michael Carrick’s side have struggled to build any momentum this season. Sunday’s 1-1 draw against Leeds extended their winless run to six matches in all competitions, leaving United with just seven points from their opening seven Premier League games.

The pressure on Carrick continues to grow. A win in Europe would offer some relief, but Como will not make life easy for Manchester United.

Manchester United began their Champions League campaign with a convincing 4-0 win over Sabah FK but lost 2-0 to Atletico Madrid in their next match. They have since drawn with Leeds, having also failed to beat Fulham and Tottenham in the Premier League.

Their last six matches across all competitions have produced three draws and three defeats. Michael Carrick is in pressure of his own and needs a response from his players, particularly with United sitting 13th in the Premier League and 13th in the Champions League standings.

Como have shown more promise. Cesc Fabregas’ side beat RB Leipzig 4-1 in Europe before losing 3-2 to Feyenoord. They returned to winning ways against Fiorentina, claiming a 3-1 victory that moved them up to fifth in Serie A, with 14 points from seven games.

Como have scored 11 goals and conceded eight across their last six matches in all competitions. United have struggled, with their only clean sheet of the season coming against Sabah FK.

United have several confirmed absentees ahead of the trip to Italy. Patrick Dorgu, Manuel Ugarte and Benjamin Sesko are ruled out, while Leny Yoro is suspended for the European fixture after picking a red against Atletico Madrid.

Lisandro Martinez is a major concern after coming off at half-time against Leeds with a thigh problem. Ayden Heaven, Luke Shaw and Kobbie Mainoo are all doubtful for the game.

Como will be without Assane Diao, who is sidelined with a thigh injury. Moise Kean has a shin problem and is a doubt, while Trevoh Chalobah is also a fitness concern with a muscular issue.

The match takes place at the Stadio Giuseppe Sinigaglia on Wednesday, October 21, with kick-off at 5:45 pm BST.

UK viewers can watch the Champions League fixture live on TNT Sports 2 and HBO Max.

#2175. Ex-Burnley, West Brom & Southampton star Jay Rodriguez names best-ever teammate

Jay Rodriguez announced his retirement last week, leaving many reminiscing over his time at Southampton, where he played a big part in their mini-Golden era in the early 2010s.

The 37-year-old scored goals wherever he went, whether that was at hometown club Burnley, West Brom or Southampton, but his best scoring season in the Premier League came at St Mary's, where he was one of the talismanic players under Mauricio Pochettino in the 2013/14 campaign.

Saints finished eighth that year, and while the Argentine left the club and numerous key players followed suit, they laid the foundations for numerous years on the fringes of, or actually getting into, Europe, and a run to the EFL Cup final in 2017.

Rodriguez scored 15 times that season, partnering with Rickie Lambert, who netted 13, with the likes of Morgan Schneiderlin, Jack Cork and a young James Ward-Prowse breaking through behind them.

But it was someone else in that Saints side whom the former striker proudly states is the best player he ever played with.

Rodriguez appeared on the 'I Had Trials Once' podcast last week to talk through his career, and spoke with Gaz Seddon and Gary Stopforth about that Southampton side, of which he made his solitary England appearance while playing in.

The trio ran through some of the players in that squad, including Nathaniel Clyne, Luke Shaw and Jose Fonte, alongside some of the names mentioned above, and Rodriguez was then asked if any of those stood out as "top" players while playing with them.

"Lallana," the ex-Saints man said, pretty easily. "I always say it in everything; he's the best I've ever played with.

Collect every point to win the round. Don’t let Neil Warnock catch you.

Swipe on the pitch or use the pad to move.

"Everything, technical, tactical, as a captain, he'd kill you if you weren't working hard in training, because he'd be working to his maximum. He's really passionate; he loves football."

Lallana was part of the Saints class who departed to 'bigger' things after that eighth-placed finish in the Premier League in 2013/14. He, Lambert and Dejan Lovren all left for Liverpool, while Luke Shaw went to Manchester United and Calum Chambers signed for Arsenal.

There's little surprise in Rodriguez stating that Lallana was the best footballer he'd ever played with, as the now-retired 38-year-old oozed class all the way from his time in League One with Southampton to the Premier League at Liverpool.

The midfielder was one of the driving forces in Saints' double promotion under Nigel Adkins, scoring 23 and assisting 15 across both League One campaigns and then registering 11 goals and 10 assists in their Championship promotion term in 2011/12.

Even the Premier League didn't seem too large a step-up, and when he moved to Anfield in 2014, he was one of the more important players in the early Jürgen Klopp days after the German boss became Liverpool manager in 2015.

Lallana netted eight and assisted seven in the 2016/17 Premier League campaign, but a hamstring injury the following year saw him miss 31 games. Unfortunately, he could never really get a lengthy run without breaking down after that as a Liverpool player.

Do you think Adam Lallana could have been a major player in Liverpool's recent golden era if not for injury? Let us know in the comments.

At Brighton and Hove Albion, he never played more than 1,600 league minutes in each of his four years there, with his minutes being managed even when he was fit to play, and he retired after a year back at Southampton during their most recent Premier League campaign in 2024/25.

Nearly a decade on from that initial hamstring injury, questions are still being asked regarding what his career could have looked like if he had remained healthy while Liverpool were starting to find their feet under Klopp, en route to becoming one of the best clubs in the World.

Rodriguez retires having been one of the more underrated goalscorers in the EFL over the 14 or so years he was in the limelight.

More often than not, he'd go under the radar towards a double-digit scoring campaign regardless of whether he was in the Championship or the Premier League, with his best year coming at West Brom in 2018/19, where both he and strike partner Dwight Gayle netted over 20 each for a Baggies side who finished in the play-offs.

Even back in 2022/23, a then-33-year-old Rodriguez netted ten for the Vincent Kompany-led Burnley side en route to the Championship title. From then, injuries and a place further down the pecking order stopped him from making much of an impact, both at Turf Moor and then at Wrexham.

Now the boots are hung up, it's fun to look back on some of the squads he was part of, but no doubt that early Southampton side in the Premier League with Adam Lallana pulling the strings in the midfield was the most entertaining.

#2174. Robinson on the brink but Aberdeen’s deep-rooted problems go far beyond the manager

Friday marked the 40th anniversary of Alex Ferguson quitting Aberdeen for Manchester United, leaving faces like granite behind him.

Media outlets wheeled out old, grainy footage from the day of mourning, as BBC cameras conveyed the lunchtime grief of shell-shocked boozers in King Street’s Pittodrie Bar.

One old boy in a flat cap condemned the lack of loyalty from a man who demanded absolute fidelity from his players. Another proffered the view that Fergie would regret a sudden rush of blood to the head. The fan who felt the move might present Aberdeen with a bit of a problem was a master of understatement.

Four decades since they lost their Napoleon, Aberdeen are a club haunted by the past. Battlefield generals like Ferguson and Willie Miller set the bar so high, those who followed were guaranteed to shoot themselves in the feet.

Read more: Haissem Hassan Celtic absence explained as ‘manoeuvring’ costs winger

The club’s last league title came in May 1985. Major trophies have been as rare as snow in April.

While no one has any expectation of European glory these days, supporters reared on tales of the halcyon days are entitled to expect more than three finishes in the bottom six of the SPFL Premiership since 2021/22.  With a staff cost base of around £16million a year, that’s a scandalous state of affairs.

Had the Beeb returned to the Pittodrie Bar after Saturday’s 4-0 hammering from Hibs, they would have found a support happy to see the latest Aberdeen manager off the premises. Had Stephen Robinson been up for a move to Manchester, they’d have revved the car and driven him south themselves.

When the Northern Irishman leaves, it won’t be by choice. It never is these days.

Under contract until 2029, managerial pay-offs have become an expensive annual event.

And, for the Dons hierarchy, it might now be time to time ask themselves an awkward question. What if all those sacked bosses were never really the problem?

In the last five years, Derek McInnes, Stephen Glass, Jim Goodwin, Barry Robson and Jimmy Thelin all left with a black bin bag tucked under their arm. Robinson will be next to collect his P45 after a hideous second-half collapse against Hibs.

The Aberdeen job is now a poisoned chalice. Hiring managers who have done well elsewhere, the club chews them up, spits them out, then watches on as they move somewhere else and remind everyone that they were never a bad boss in the first place.

McInnes came to within minutes of a league title at Hearts last season and is now breathing down the necks of Celtic as manager of Rangers.

While Glass was always an odd, left-field choice, he had a useful two years at USL Championship side Memphis 901 and was last seen serving as Robbie Keane’s assistant at Ferencvaros.

Goodwin recovered from an ignominious Scottish Cup calamity in Darvel to prove himself a better manager than he looked the day he walked across the Easter Road pitch with a man bag over his shoulder after a 6-0 defeat to Hibs. Dundee United are now a club five places and six points better off than Aberdeen.

Cork City were promoted to the League of Ireland Premier Division last month, earning Barry Robson a new two-year contract in the process.

Two years ago this week, Jimmy Thelin had Aberdeen joint-top of the Premiership after 11 games of the 2024/25 season. Since then, the team have played 77 league games and won 19. That’s a win rate of just 25 per cent.

Supporters never really wanted Robinson in the first place. The people running the club never seemed sold on him either.

The plan was to make an overseas appointment, with Eirik Horneland the preferred candidate in March. When talks with the Norwegian stalled, Sandro Schwarz flew in to watch a game against Celtic, took one look and decided he was better off moving to Moscow.

A solid operator at Motherwell and St Mirren, Robinson was the last man standing at the bar.

Portrayed – harshly – as a long-ball, survival specialist, there was always a question over his ability to win hearts and minds at Aberdeen. To convince the critics he had to hit the ground running and, despite scratching a win over Hearts, that didn’t happen.

A thumping 4-0 win in Motherwell in September proved a false dawn when stats showed that the Dons converted all four of their shots on target and enjoyed possession of just 31 per cent.

Since Fir Park, they have won just once in seven games, against St Mirren. And the Northern Irishman’s demeanour has grown progressively more pained. Weekly monologues on the need to be better have lost any impact.

The first big decision for new chief executive Adrian Bevington, there is a grim inevitability to how this ends and wherever he turns up next, Robinson will do what so many former Aberdeen managers do by displaying a talent for winning games of football at another club. As with so many before, it won’t happen in the Granite City.

A club which sucks the life from promising careers, an Aberdeen manager is only ever two bad games from the sack. The man in the technical area works in a culture of fear, fulfilling the role of human shield for senior figures wary of sticking their head over the parapet.

Non-executive chairman Dave Cormack is a passionate fan in the boardroom. After open-heart surgery three years ago, he tried to take a step back by appointing a chief executive to run the show. Alan Burrows has now gone and every Aberdeen departure – for there are many – turns the finger of accusation turn in Cormack’s direction.

No one can accuse the chairman of failing to back his managers. The Dons have spent substantial sums building, then rebuilding, failing teams. How much they spend is less of a problem than how they spend it.

Sporting director Lutz Pfannenstiel was hired to bring strategic and continental know-how. And, at first, the German seemed keen to make himself the centre of attention.

Last season, he was parked beside interim boss Peter Leven in the dugout. These days, you could stand on the Beach Boulevard with a set of strong binoculars and struggle to find his dot on the North Sea horizon.

In Scottish football there is a new unwritten rule. Hearts and Aberdeen, it seems, can never be successful in the same season and, while the Tynecastle club have established themselves as the third force in Scottish football – Falkirk not withstanding – Aberdeen labour in the relegation play-off place.

When Robinson goes, expect the next guy to be an overseas appointment. A blameless optimist who vaguely remembers Aberdeen winning a European trophy in the days when he was knee-high to a grasshopper, and sees a club which can – and should – be so much more than the blazing bin fire it is now.

Rio Ferdinand has admitted he is disappointed that Manchester United failed to sign Ayyoub Bouaddi, with the highly-rated midfielder now making an impression at Manchester City.

Manchester City beat several rivals to secure Bouaddi’s signature over the summer in a deal worth £86 million. The Morocco international became the Premier League’s most expensive teenager, and Rio Ferdinand believes Manchester United missed out on a special talent.

The former United defender was particularly impressed by Bouaddi’s second-half cameo during City’s Champions League defeat to Paris Saint-Germain last week. His performance reminded Rio Ferdinand why he had been talking about the youngster throughout the previous year and during the summer transfer window.

Speaking on his YouTube channel, Ferdinand highlighted how Bouaddi was the highlight of the game against PSG and who they missed.

“He came on and showed PSG that they may have missed out on someone who was on their doorstep when he was playing in France,” Ferdinand said.

The former England international also confirmed that Manchester United had been interested in bringing the midfielder to Old Trafford, but the transfer fee was too expensive.

“Manchester United were in for him, 100%, but the fee was just too much,” he added.

Ferdinand was left frustrated by what he saw from the teenager, who turned 19 this month.

“Just that little cameo against PSG makes you go, ‘oh, I can’t believe we missed out on that. I can’t believe it.’ I’m so gutted, so gutted. He’s bad! He’s so calm under pressure.”

Rio Ferdinand suggested Bouaddi’s quality could soon make the midfield position in a packed Manchester City his regular role.

City already have Elliot Anderson and Enzo Fernandez among their midfield options, but Ferdinand believes Bouaddi has the ability to stand out alongside them.

“They’ve got Elliot Anderson and Enzo Fernandez in that midfield as well but this kid could be the best of the three, easily.”

#2172. Chelsea teenager Reggie Watson captains England and scores as Germany snatch victory with late comeback

Graduate Sports Journalist with a love for football.

Chelsea midfielder Reggie Watson scored while captaining England Under-17s on Sunday, although Germany’s late comeback ended his international window with a 3-2 defeat.

The 16-year-old equalised from the penalty spot after Oscar Johnson drew a foul inside the area.

According to England’s official match report, Watson beat goalkeeper Nick Hartung with a finish into the left-hand corner.

Mylo Bernard put England ahead on the hour, but Linus Güther equalised seven minutes later. Niko Ilicevic then struck the winner in the 83rd minute.

Barry Lewtas’ side finished the three-match tournament with two victories and one defeat, having previously beaten Israel and Venezuela.

Watson’s involvement offers Chelsea supporters another opportunity to track a teenager already introduced to senior football by Xabi Alonso.

As covered in our report on Watson’s first-team progress, he started the Carabao Cup victory over Leeds United and played the opening 45 minutes.

That appearance, aged 16 years and 226 days, placed him fourth among Chelsea’s youngest competitive debutants.

His England captaincy and goal add a concrete international development to that emerging club story.
